Courage is thus a form of trust, exercised as much in endurance as in daring.

--- Buddhism — reframed ---

Fear arises from clinging — to self, possessions, reputation — so fearlessness is not bravado but the fruit of releasing what fear protects. The gift of fearlessness (abhaya-dana), making others safe from oneself, is counted a form of generosity.
  • The greatest conquest is of oneself — valor turned inward. [C3]

      — Dhp 103 — The Dhammapada, trans. F. Max Müller (1881)

  • The boundless friendly mind is the settled state in which fear has no foothold. [C4]
      “As a mother at the risk of her life watches over her own child, her only child, so also let every one cultivate a boundless (friendly) mind towards all beings.”

--- Hinduism — encouraged ---
Courage in the Gita is svadharma enacted: for the warrior, valour and not slinking from battle are natural duties, and Arjuna's despair is answered not with comfort but with a summons to act. The deeper teaching universalizes it — do your duty without attachment to outcomes — making fearlessness a fruit of surrendered action rather than confidence in results.
  • Valour and steadfastness in battle are the kshatriya's natural duties. [C5]
      “Valour, glory, courage, dexterity, not slinking away from battle, gifts, exercise of lordly power, these are the natural duties of a Kshatriya, born of (his) own nature.”

--- Confucianism — encouraged ---

We suffer more often in imagination than in reality: most fear is anticipatory fiction, and the Stoic drill is to test the projection against the present fact. Courage is one of the four virtues, but it begins as epistemology — death is not terrible, the opinion is — and matures as practice: premeditation of adversity, voluntary discomfort, and the steady recollection of what is and is not in your power.

      “The man, then, who faces and who fears the right things and from the right motive, in the right way and at the right time, and who feels confidence under the corresponding conditions, is brave; for the brave man feels and acts according to the merits of the case and in whatever way the rule directs.”
      — NE III.7, 1115b17 — The Nicomachean Ethics, trans. W. D. Ross (1925)

  • Five counterfeits are catalogued, each resembling the real thing in the deed and differing in what moves it. [C12]
      “Courage, then, is something of this sort, but the name is also applied to five other kinds. First comes the courage of the citizen-soldier; for this is most like true courage.”
      — NE III.8, 1116a17 — The Nicomachean Ethics, trans. W. D. Ross (1925)
      Context: Aristotle catalogues five counterfeits of courage, including action from legal penalty, from experience, from spirit, from optimism and from ignorance. Each resembles bravery in the deed and differs in the motive.
  • Fear is not explained away: death is granted to be the most terrible thing, since it is the end. [C13]
      “Now death is the most terrible of all things; for it is the end, and nothing is thought to be any longer either good or bad for the dead.”
      — NE III.6, 1115a26 — The Nicomachean Ethics, trans. W. D. Ross (1925)
